# What "More Productive" Means

::: {.callout-note}

-   Explain why "productivity" is a definition problem before it is a
    measurement problem.
-   Judge whether a metric actually captures the thing it claims to measure.
-   Recognize the classic proxy-metric traps and Goodhart's Law.
-   Reproduce how the "10x programmer" claim collapses as the definition
    tightens.

:::

Back at Meridian, Dev has a number for the CTO ready to go: *pull requests
merged per week.* It went up 18% after the AI tool shipped, so the tool is
working. Case closed.

Maya asks the one question that stops the room: *"Working at what?"*

Before you can measure whether AI makes programmers more productive, you have
to decide what "productive" means — and that turns out to be the hard part. A
2021 Microsoft paper called SPACE argued that developer productivity has at
least five dimensions — satisfaction, performance, activity, communication, and
efficiency-and-flow — and that optimizing one (say, commit frequency) routinely
degrades the others [@Forsgren2021]. If you only measure what is easy to count,
you optimize for the wrong thing.

## Construct Validity: Does the Number Mean What You Think It Means?

{{<g construct_validity "Construct validity" >}} is the degree to which a
measurement actually captures the concept it is supposed to capture. A metric
has high construct validity when changes in the metric reliably reflect changes
in the thing you care about.

Productivity is unusually hard to operationalize. In manufacturing it means
"widgets per hour" — output and time are both measurable. Software output is not
homogeneous: a ten-line bugfix can be worth more than a thousand-line feature, or
vice versa. Much of the work is invisible (reading code, reviewing, helping a
colleague). The effects are delayed (a shortcut today becomes defects in six
months). And most of a developer's day isn't even writing code: a field study
tracking developers for two weeks found coding occupied roughly a quarter of the
day, with meetings and coordination consuming the rest [@Meyer2017].

The consequence: construct validity is usually *assumed* rather than
*demonstrated*, especially in industry studies. Dev's "PRs per week" is a
perfect example — it's a number, but it isn't "productivity."

## Proxy Metrics and How They Go Wrong

A {{<g proxy_metric "proxy metric" >}} is a measurable quantity you use as a
stand-in for something harder to measure. The usual proxies for developer
productivity, and the way each one gets gamed:

-   **Lines of code** — incentivizes verbosity; punishes refactoring and
    deletion. In 1982, Apple tracked LOC until Bill Atkinson deleted ~2,000
    lines of QuickDraw in one week and management stopped asking
    [@Sadowski2019].
-   **Commit frequency** — incentivizes small, meaningless commits.
-   **Story points completed** — incentivizes inflating the estimates.
-   **Pull requests merged** — incentivizes trivial PRs and discourages hard
    work.
-   **Bugs closed** — incentivizes closing without fixing.

There's a name for the general phenomenon. {{<g goodharts_law "Goodhart's Law" >}}
says that *when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure*
[@Goodhart1984]. The moment people know they're being scored on commit count,
they make more, smaller commits. The number improves; the work does not. The
same trap bedevils AI-productivity studies, which is why the next chapter treats
it as the first mistake to watch for.

::: {.callout-note}

In the early 1980s, Apple measured programmer productivity by lines of code per
day. Bill Atkinson, who wrote the QuickDraw graphics library, once submitted a
timesheet showing **-2000 lines**: he'd replaced 2,000 lines with a faster,
shorter algorithm. The metric penalized the improvement [@Sadowski2019].

:::

## Watch the "10x Programmer" Collapse

The best way to see that "productivity" is a definition, not a fact, is to do
the arithmetic yourself. In 2000 Lutz Prechelt measured a mix of students and
professionals, using seven different languages, as they each solved the *same*
small algorithmic problem [@Prechelt2000]. The raw data is in
`data/prechelt.csv` — one row per person, with the language (`lang`), work time
in hours (`whours`), and several quality metrics.

Start with the crudest possible claim: *the fastest programmer is N times faster
than the slowest.* Compute the minimum and maximum work time and take the ratio.
You'll get something like **105x**. Is there really a 105x programmer? Almost
certainly not — that ratio compares the single fastest person to the single
slowest, and the slowest "came back every day for a week."

Now tighten the definition the way a careful researcher would:

1. **Homogeneous language.** The mix of seven languages confounds the
   comparison (some languages suit the task better). Filter to just the Java
   rows. The ratio drops to about **17x**.
2. **Compare the top 10% to the ordinary, not the worst.** "Faster than normal
   programmers" should mean "faster than the slower half." Compare the median of
   the top 10% (the 5th percentile) to the median of the bottom half (the 75th
   percentile). The ratio drops again — to around **11x**, and under some
   reasonable definitions to **5x**.
3. **Factor in quality.** "Productivity" isn't just speed — it's value per
   effort. The `z1000rel` column is a reliability score (100 is perfect, lower
   means more defects), and `z1000mem` is memory use. Once you fold in "did it
   actually work?", the picture changes again.

The lesson isn't "there are no fast programmers." It's that *the answer depends
on the question,* and a number that moves by a factor of 20 depending on how you
ask is not a fact about the world — it's a fact about your definition.

## The Grown-Up Version: SPACE and DORA

If single metrics are hopeless, what do serious teams use?

**SPACE** (Satisfaction-and-well-being, Performance, Activity, Communication,
Efficiency-and-flow) is a framework for remembering that productivity has
multiple dimensions and that they trade off [@Forsgren2021]. **DORA** — the
DevOps Research and Assessment program — found four metrics that correlate with
*organizational* delivery performance: deployment frequency, lead time for
changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service [@Forsgren2018]. DORA
metrics have better construct validity than raw activity counts because they tie
to customer outcomes rather than to keystrokes.

Both are still imperfect. A team can score beautifully on DORA while building
the wrong product, and neither framework will tell you whether the AI tool —
specifically — is helping. What they give you is the right *question* to ask:
which dimension are we trying to move, and how would we know?

## Misconceptions

Writing more code means being more productive.
:   Wrong in both directions: deleting a thousand lines of tangled code and
    replacing them with a hundred clear ones improves the codebase, not harms it.

If a metric improves, the thing it measures must be improving.
:   Goodhart's Law kicks in the moment people know they're being measured.
    Better-looking numbers are often just behavior change around the measurement.

Productivity is an objective property you can measure with the right data.
:   Every operationalization embeds a choice about what matters — speed, quality,
    satisfaction, business value. Those are values choices, not measurement
    problems.

DORA metrics measure individual developer productivity.
:   They measure team and organizational delivery. Using them to grade an
    individual conflates levels of analysis and ignores the system factors that
    dominate individual variation.

Better measurement tools produce better management.
:   Measurement is not management. Even complete data needs judgment to act on,
    and improving productivity requires behavior change, not more dashboards
    [@Sadowski2019].

## Check Understanding

<details markdown="1">
<summary markdown="1">What is construct validity, and why does it matter for a productivity metric?</summary>

Construct validity is how well a measurement captures the concept it's meant to
represent. It matters because a low-validity metric will mislead you: you can
improve the number without improving the thing you care about. "Commits per day"
has low construct validity — developers can raise it while becoming *less*
productive.

</details>

<details markdown="1">
<summary markdown="1">Dev says "PRs merged per week went up 18%, so the tool is working." Give two specific threats to that conclusion.</summary>

First, PRs-per-week is a low-validity proxy: developers respond to being
measured by splitting work into smaller PRs without delivering more value.
Second, it's a before-and-after comparison with no control group, so any
concurrent change (team growth, a new CI, a backlog cleanup) could explain the
rise.

</details>

<details markdown="1">
<summary markdown="1">In the Prechelt data, why does the "fastest vs slowest" ratio (about 105x) overstate real differences between programmers?</summary>

Because it compares the single fastest person to the single slowest, and the
slowest person is an outlier who took "every day for a week." Tightening the
definition — restricting to one language, comparing the top 10% to the *typical*
programmer rather than the worst, and folding in quality — collapses the ratio
to roughly 5x–17x. The headline number is an artifact of the definition.

</details>

## Exercises

### The Prechelt Data Lab (25 minutes, solo or pairs)

Load `data/prechelt.csv` into a spreadsheet or a short script. Compute, and
write down each number:

1.  The min and max `whours`, and their ratio.
2.  The same ratio restricted to `lang == "Java"`.
3.  The 5th and 75th percentiles of `whours` across all rows, and their ratio.
4.  The same percentiles restricted to Java, and their ratio.

Then answer in one sentence: *which of these is the "right" answer to "how much
faster is a fast programmer than a normal one" — and why does it depend on your
definition?*

### Operationalize It (15 minutes, pairs)

Pick one of — *code quality, developer satisfaction, onboarding effectiveness* —
and write a specific, measurable definition for it. Then write one paragraph on
how your definition could be gamed (i.e., improved without the underlying thing
improving). Trade with a partner and try to game *their* definition.

### Goodhart in the Wild (10 minutes, solo)

Think of a metric you've seen used to judge developer performance. Describe one
concrete way someone could improve the number without improving the work. If you
can't think of one from your own job, use "number of tickets closed per sprint."
